newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to launch French justice reform on TV.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to launch French justice reform on TV.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, keen to distract voters from record unemployment and funding scandals in his Gaullist party, planned to launch a major reform of France's justice system in a broadcast on Monday.
The president has said the reform will be one of the key initiatives of his seven-year term, following last year's overhaul of the armed forces with the abolition of conscription.

Chirac's office said he would set the terms of reference of a commission, which will have six months to propose ways of guaranteeing judicial independence, protecting the right of suspects to be presumed innocent and making the civil and penal justice system more user-friendly.
The Justice Ministry announced a bipartisan panel of 21 jurists, academics, civil servants and journalists to be headed by Supreme Court president Pierre Truche.

They included the chairman of the Agence France-Presse news agency, Jean Miot, the editor of Roman Catholic daily La Croix, Noel Copin, philosophers Blandine Barret-Kriegel and Luc Ferry, Supreme Court prosecutor Jean-Francois Burgelin and a former aide to the late president Francois Mitterrand, Jean Kahn.

Under fire over alleged government meddling in justice investigations concerning political corruption, Chirac raised the prospect in a December 12 interview of cutting the umbilical cord between the judiciary and France's political authorities.

"I think that today we must seriously examine the possibility of making the public prosecutor's office independent of the justice minister," the president said. He acknowledged doubts about the freedom of magistrates to prosecute political corruption without interference.

He also said the commission should study ways of upholding the presumption of innocence, which he said was "constantly flouted" by the publication of details of investigations before a suspect was brought to trial, and steps to simplify legal procedures for ordinary citizens seeking redress.

Magistrates are investigating evidence that the Gaullist RPR party systematically took rake-offs in exchange for housing and public works contrats in the Paris region while Chirac was mayor from 1977 to 1995.
Several businessmen and fundraisers, including former RPR personnel chief Louise-Yvonne Casetta, have been placed under judicial investigation but none has yet been brought to trial.

Political analysts said Chirac's initiative had the dual advantage of disarming criticism over these probes and diverting national debate from economic stagnation, unemployment, deficit cutting and the single European currency.

Since it concerned the separation of powers between the executive and the judiciary, it might require a constitutional amendment, which could give the president the opportunity for a winnable referendum later this year, if he so chose, they said.

Since the government could not enact an amnesty for party funding offences, which proved politically disastrous for its Socialist predecessors in 1990, it could at least show it was doing its best to clean up the justice system.
However, some members of the centre-right coalition have expressed doubts about making the judiciary independent.

Senior jurists such as parliamentary legal committee chairman Pierre Mazeaud have warned of a "government of judges" and questioned how magistrates would draw their legitimacy if they were not appointed by elected political authorities.

Jean-Marie le Pen, leader of the extreme-right National Front, said he was not convinced judges were more trustworthy than politicians. "At least we can judge politicians through elections. How could we judge the magistrates and where would their legitimacy come from?" he asked.

The Higher Magistrates' Council, which recommends senior judicial appointments to the president, submitted a memorandum to Chirac last week suggesting two relatively simple measures would be sufficient to guarantee judicial independence.

It said the justice ministry should no longer appoint or promote prosecutors and magistrates, whose careers would be managed by the independent council, and the minister should be barred from giving orders to prosecutors in individual cases.
Opposition Socialist party spokesman Francois Hollande said there was no need for the Truche commission since the president only needed to follow the council's advice.
